title: Central Bank Holds at 37% as Oil Shock Tests Inflation Fight, CHP Mass Exodus Takes Shape, Greece Buys Israeli Air Shield
subhead: Turkey's central bank left rates unchanged for a fourth straight meeting as oil's return above $100 and Red Sea tanker attacks add energy-cost pressure to an already fragile inflation outlook. Ninety-five of 135 CHP lawmakers declared support for Ozgur Ozel's new party. And Greece approved a €3.5 billion Israeli air defense system — the latest regional arms buildup reshaping the Eastern Mediterranean balance.

sections.heading: Central Bank Holds at 37%, Flags Geopolitical Risk
sections.body:
Turkey's central bank left its benchmark one-week repo rate at 37% for a fourth consecutive meeting on July 23, as widely expected. The Monetary Policy Committee noted that the underlying inflation trend declined only modestly in June, with a temporary uptick expected in July due to rising energy costs from the Middle East conflict.

The decision statement highlighted two countervailing forces: domestic demand weakening on one hand, and energy prices rebounding on the other due to the Iran war and its ripple effects through the Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea. The overnight borrowing rate was held at 34% and the lending rate at 40%.

Economists broadly read the statement as a signal that rate cuts remain on the table but are contingent on geopolitical conditions improving. Former CBRT chief economist Hakan Kara said the more explicit language about domestic demand weakening means 'rate cuts are still on the table, but only if geopolitics permits.' Economist Iris Cibre maintained her year-end rate forecast at 34% and inflation at 29%, but warned she would revise both if the war extends past August and energy prices keep climbing.

Baskent University economist Senol Babuscu pointed to a striking structural indicator: the 200-lira note now accounts for 90% of the total value of banknotes in circulation, up from just 5.5% in 2009 — a measure of how far the lira's purchasing power has eroded even as headline inflation declines.
sections.whyItMatters: The hold was expected, but the statement's emphasis on geopolitical energy risk is a shift — the CBRT is effectively saying the war, not domestic fundamentals, now sets the timeline for easing. Every dollar added to oil imports widens the current account deficit and delays the rate cuts Turkey's economy needs.

sections.heading: CHP Fracture Formalizes: 95 of 135 MPs Back Ozel's New Party
sections.body:
An overwhelming majority of CHP lawmakers — 95 of 135 — have publicly declared support for Ozgur Ozel's plan to establish a new party, according to a review of lawmakers' social media accounts by Bianet. Only 21 MPs backed reinstated leader Kemal Kilicdaroglu, while 18 have not publicly stated a position.

If the new party registers, it would immediately become the second-largest group in parliament after the ruling AKP, which now holds 277 seats after a string of opposition defections. The rump CHP would drop to seventh place.

The split traces to a May court ruling that invalidated the CHP's November 2023 leadership congress, removed Ozel as chairman, and reinstated Kilicdaroglu — who had led the party for 14 years before losing to Ozel. Ozel's faction appealed to the Court of Cassation, but the case was not taken up before the judicial recess that began July 20. Ozel also accused Kilicdaroglu's camp of refusing to convene an extraordinary party congress despite meeting the delegate petition threshold.

The opposition crisis extends beyond the CHP. Istanbul Mayor Ekrem Imamoglu — Ozel's declared presidential candidate — has been imprisoned since March 2025 on corruption and espionage charges he denies. Authorities have expanded investigations to CHP-run municipalities, suspending dozens of mayors including those of Antalya, Adana, and Bursa. The government says the investigations are independent; the opposition calls them politically motivated.
sections.whyItMatters: Turkey's main opposition is now formally split between a rump CHP led by Kilicdaroglu and a new party commanding the bulk of its parliamentary caucus. The AKP gains a stronger hand in a fragmented parliament, while the opposition enters 2028 election planning divided.

sections.heading: Court Bans DW Journalist's X Account After Release
sections.body:
Days after Deutsche Welle correspondent Alican Uludag was released under judicial control following 25 hours in custody, an Ankara court ordered an access ban on his X account and 13 specific posts, according to the Freedom of Expression Association (IFOD). X has made all 13 posts inaccessible in Turkey but has not restricted access to the account itself.

The ban was issued under Article 8/A of Law No. 5651, on grounds of 'protecting national security and public order.' The restricted posts included Uludag's criticism of the detention of actor Levent Uzumcu, questions about political and military responsibility around the 2016 coup attempt, reporting on investigations targeting journalists, and commentary on operations against CHP-run municipalities and the imprisonment of Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality media director Fatos Pinar Turker.

The access ban extends the legal pressure on Uludag, who was already facing trial in a separate case for 'insulting the president' and was detained July 21 over a social media post criticizing Turkey's judicial system. He is under an international travel ban and required to report to police four times a week.
sections.whyItMatters: The access ban converts detention into a more durable form of censorship — rendering reporting permanently inaccessible rather than just temporarily silencing the journalist. It marks a further expansion of Article 8/A as a tool for suppressing critical coverage of the judiciary and security establishment.

sections.heading: Red Sea Tanker Attacks Compound Turkey's Energy Cost Squeeze
sections.body:
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels claimed responsibility for attacks on two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea on July 23, according to AP. The strikes pushed Brent crude above $100 per barrel — a roughly 40% increase this month alone — and triggered a doubling of war risk insurance costs for southern Red Sea voyages, according to Reuters.

The attacks open a second chokepoint beyond Hormuz. If the Bab el-Mandeb Strait becomes impassable for commercial shipping, it would block the Red Sea-Suez Canal route that handles roughly 10% of global trade — and force all Asia-Europe container traffic around the Cape of Good Hope, adding weeks and cost.

For Turkey, the energy math is direct: the country imports almost all of its energy needs, as Istanbul-based economist Atilla Yesilada told Xinhua. Sustained high oil prices feed directly into inflation and widen the current account deficit — the same dynamics that led the CBRT to keep rates at 37%.

At the same time, the disruption adds urgency to pipeline projects that bypass maritime chokepoints. Iraq is pursuing plans to route southern oil from Basra to Turkey's Mediterranean port of Ceyhan, with a branch extending to Baniyas in Syria, according to CBS News. The US State Department has called the Iraq-Turkey route 'a critical energy corridor.' Goldman Sachs estimates new bypass projects could carry an additional 3.8 million barrels per day by end-2027.
sections.whyItMatters: Turkey's energy import bill rises with every dollar added to oil, directly pressuring the inflation outlook the CBRT is trying to manage. But the same disruption increases the strategic value of Turkey's pipeline infrastructure — making Ceyhan more important with each passing week of Hormuz and Red Sea disruption.

sections.heading: Greenlights €3.5B 'Achilles Shield' With Israeli Tech
sections.body:
Greece's top security council (KYSEA) is set to approve the €3.5 billion 'Achilles Shield' air defense program, integrating Israeli radar and missile systems from Rafael Advanced Defense Systems and Israel Aerospace Industries, according to RaillyNews. The system will create a layered network capable of intercepting threats from drones to ballistic missiles.

The program replaces Greece's aging Russian S-300 systems — which face maintenance and parts challenges — and integrates with existing US Patriot batteries to form a cohesive multi-tier network. Deployment will focus on key military bases, maritime chokepoints, energy facilities, and urban centers, with particular emphasis on areas facing 'regional adversaries' — a clear reference to Turkey's assertive posture in the Aegean and Eastern Mediterranean.

The move deepens a trend: as Turkey's F-35 acquisition remains blocked and its defense posture becomes more assertive, Greece is investing heavily in interoperable NATO-standard systems from Israel and the US. The Achilles Shield follows Greece's recent acquisition of F-35s and French Belharra frigates — a multi-billion-euro modernization that is widening the qualitative gap in Greece's favor in the Aegean air domain.
sections.whyItMatters: Every Greek arms purchase that closes the capability gap with Turkey strengthens Athens' negotiating position on maritime disputes — and increases the cost of any Turkish escalation in the Aegean or around Cyprus. The Oruc Reis surveys and the Achilles Shield are two sides of the same Eastern Mediterranean competition.

sections.heading: Iraq-Turkey Pipeline Gains Strategic Urgency as Hormuz Bypass Accelerates
sections.body:
As Gulf states race to build alternatives to the Strait of Hormuz, the Iraq-to-Turkey pipeline route is gaining renewed strategic momentum. Iraqi officials are ramping up plans for a pipeline from Basra to Ceyhan on Turkey's Mediterranean coast, with a branch to Baniyas in Syria, according to CBS News. The US State Department has called the Iraq-Ceyhan route 'a critical energy corridor,' and $200 billion in deals were recently signed between Iraq's Oil Ministry and American companies during Prime Minister Ali AlZaidi's visit to Washington.

Analysts at Goldman Sachs estimate that combined new pipeline projects could carry an additional 3.8 million barrels per day by end-2027 and 7.3 million barrels per day by end-2028, meaning roughly 60% of prewar Gulf exports could eventually bypass Hormuz.

For Turkey, the strategic calculus is straightforward: every barrel rerouted from Hormuz to Ceyhan or through Turkish territory increases Ankara's leverage as an energy transit state and generates transit fees. The existing Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline, which Iraq had already been using to triple exports in recent months, becomes more valuable as alternative routes struggle to keep pace with the volumes that Hormuz once handled.
sections.whyItMatters: The Iran war is doing more to validate Turkey's energy corridor strategy than any diplomatic campaign could. But the strategic upside comes with a timing risk — Turkey still pays today's oil import prices while waiting for tomorrow's pipeline revenue.

bottomLine: Turkey's central bank kept rates at 37% for a fourth straight meeting, effectively blaming the Iran war for delaying rate cuts — an honest signal that geopolitics, not domestic policy, now sets the timeline for monetary easing. The opposition fractured further as 95 of 135 CHP lawmakers followed Ozgur Ozel into a new party, while courts extended censorship of DW journalist Uludag by banning his X account. On the regional chessboard, Greece's €3.5B Achilles Shield air defense deal with Israel and Houthi tanker strikes pushing oil above $100 both ratchet up pressure on Turkey from opposite directions — the first narrowing the Aegean military gap, the second widening the current account deficit. The one winner in Turkey's portfolio: the Iraq-Ceyhan pipeline, whose strategic value compounds with every week of Hormuz and Red Sea disruption.
sources: Xinhua, Bianet, DW, IFOD, Bloomberg, Reuters, AP, CBS News, Goldman Sachs, RaillyNews, Dunya, BBC Turkish, Morning Star, AzerNews, Euractiv, Indicator.gr, Turkish Minute
